Consistency.justification: The proposal closely follows the supplied idea: it centers on retina-inspired dynamic gazing, an agile external-cavity laser, reconfigurable electro-optic frequency-comb channels, camera-guided adaptive sensing, and hardware-efficient 4D imaging. The hypothesis, architecture, experiments, and ablations all target the stated goal of reducing global oversampling through ROI-aware allocation. However, there are some internal mismatches. The architecture is described primarily as coherent frequency-comb LiDAR, while much of the experimental design uses pulsed time-of-flight concepts such as VCSEL pulses, TDC bins, photon-counting IRFs, and EM deconvolution. The relationship among the 905 nm VCSEL fovea, 1550 nm assist channel, external-cavity laser, and electro-optic comb is not fully reconciled. It is also not made explicit how frequency channels become independently steerable spatial ROI channels. These gaps prevent perfect consistency despite strong alignment with the high-level idea.

Clarity.justification: The proposal clearly identifies the problem, states a quantitative hypothesis, lists relevant baselines and metrics, defines several acceptance thresholds, and provides a sensible hierarchy of FPGA, controller, and planner loops. The experimental factors and ablations are also easy to follow. Nevertheless, important technical details remain ambiguous. The optical path and sensing modality are not specified end to end, including whether ranging is FMCW, pulsed time-of-flight, or a hybrid. The mechanism that maps individual comb lines to separate beams or ROIs is omitted, as are the roles of the OPA, MEMS device, VCSEL, and external-cavity laser in the final prototype. Terms such as token throughput and useful bit are insufficiently defined for a LiDAR system, and posterior entropy reduction requires a precise probabilistic model and estimator. The proposal is therefore understandable at the system-concept level but not yet sufficiently defined for direct implementation or reproduction.

Novelty.justification: The strongest novel element is the proposed integration of retina-inspired ROI allocation with reconfigurable electro-optic comb channels and a closed-loop hardware control hierarchy. Adaptive scanning, camera-guided saliency, coherent LiDAR, frequency-comb parallelization, and foveated sensing each have substantial precedent, but their hardware-software co-design around dynamically reassigned comb resources could constitute a meaningful new combination. Evaluating information-per-Joule together with tail latency and perception constraints is also a useful systems contribution. The novelty is not yet demonstrated decisively because the related-work discussion is broad and contains no specific comparisons to the closest integrated frequency-comb, wavelength-steered, foveated, or camera-cooperative LiDAR systems. Moreover, the proposal does not explain the photonic mechanism that makes per-ROI comb-line reconfiguration distinct from ordinary wavelength multiplexing or adaptive beam scheduling. Thus, the concept appears notably original but not yet established as groundbreaking.

Soundness.justification: The proposal has several rigorous features: quantitative acceptance criteria, multiple baselines, controlled synthetic and real experiments, latency percentiles, ablations, ground-truth instrumentation, and explicit consideration of ambient light, reflectance, motion, and multipath. A TDC bin size of at most 50 ps is compatible with centimeter-scale quantization, although total RMSE will also depend on jitter, calibration, photon statistics, target geometry, and synchronization. Major methodological gaps reduce the score. Frequency channels do not inherently provide independently steerable spatial channels, so a wavelength-to-angle mapping or per-line routing architecture must be specified and calibrated. The coherent-comb framing is technically disconnected from the photon-counting pulsed-ToF evaluation. The information-per-Joule metric counts posterior entropy reduction per transmit energy, which may exclude laser tuning, comb generation, thermal control, detectors, FPGA processing, MEMS actuation, camera processing, and host computation; this could bias the claimed hardware-efficiency gain. The entropy estimator, prior, task representation, and definition of a bit are not given. Comparable latency, field of view, coverage, detection probability, false-alarm rate, and output quality across baselines are also not fully controlled. Statistical testing is limited to p less than 0.05 without power analysis, confidence intervals, effect-size treatment, scene-level independence, or correction across many conditions. Eye-safety compliance is recognized but lacks a wavelength-specific standard, aperture assumptions, exposure model, and validation protocol.

Feasibility.justification: Many individual components are available with current technology, including tunable narrow-linewidth lasers, electro-optic comb generators, MEMS steering, high-resolution TDCs, FPGAs, PCIe streaming, synchronized cameras, and motion-capture ground truth. The staged control architecture and hardware-in-the-loop testing make an initial laboratory demonstrator plausible. However, integrating these components into a genuinely chip-scale, coherent, reconfigurable multi-ROI system is substantially harder than the proposal suggests. Independent routing or angular steering of multiple comb lines, coherent calibration, wavelength-dependent beam pointing, optical amplification, receiver demultiplexing, thermal stabilization, crosstalk control, and simultaneous dual-wavelength eye-safety compliance are not designed in detail. An external-cavity laser and mixed 905 nm and 1550 nm prototype may also weaken the chip-scale claim. The cited FPGA buffers and PCIe interface do not establish that worst-case photon-event and token rates can be sustained. Achieving all targets simultaneously, especially a threefold energy gain, 3 cm RMSE, real-time adaptation, and eye-safe operation, carries considerable integration risk. A benchtop proof of concept is feasible, but the complete claimed platform would likely require substantial engineering and scope refinement.

Significance.justification: Reducing the energy and bandwidth cost of high-resolution 4D sensing is important for autonomous vehicles, robotics, drones, and edge machine vision. A successful system that reallocates physical sensing channels according to scene value while preserving range precision and bounded latency could improve both photonic efficiency and downstream perception efficiency. The emphasis on end-to-end control, tail latency, multipath, ambient robustness, and eye safety addresses practical concerns often omitted from algorithm-only adaptive sensing studies. The impact could be substantial if the threefold gain is measured using total system energy and demonstrated on representative perception tasks. The score is below the top range because the current evaluation does not specify task-level outcomes such as detection, tracking, or planning accuracy, and adaptive gazing can miss unexpected objects outside selected ROIs. The proposed information metric may therefore not yet establish real-world safety or perception benefit.

strengths: Strong alignment with the retina-inspired adaptive LiDAR idea and a clear quantitative hypothesis involving energy, range accuracy, and latency.
Broad experimental plan with synthetic and real data, relevant baselines, ablations, tail-latency measurements, and explicit risk recognition.
Potentially valuable integration of reconfigurable frequency-comb photonics with closed-loop camera-guided sensing.
Addresses an important systems problem with meaningful potential impact in energy-constrained 4D machine vision.
weaknesses: The optical architecture is under-specified, particularly how comb frequencies map to independently steerable ROI channels.
There is a significant mismatch between the coherent frequency-comb framing and the pulsed photon-counting, TDC, IRF, and VCSEL-based experimental methodology.
The information-per-Joule definition excludes or does not clearly include major system energy costs and lacks a reproducible entropy-estimation protocol.
Fairness controls, statistical power, eye-safety validation, task-level perception metrics, and safeguards against missed non-salient objects require substantial development.
